topics: 🦌 The Koy's Extended Prohibitions — blood, fat, carcass, and sciatic nerve, all derived from a distinct creature
🐓 Why 'Bird AND Animal'? — the generalization-detail exegesis behind the blood prohibition's scope
🧑 Does Human Flesh Ever Carry 'Light' Impurity? — reconciling a mishna about cutting flesh from a living person
🩸 Marginal Cases: Fish Blood, Human Blood, Creeping Things — how collection, warning, and species-marks change the ruling
🍞 Combining Less Than an Olive-Bulk — when a sliver of carcass and a bit of food together reach the impurity threshold

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Mapping the Edges of the Blood Prohibition
overview.subtitle: Keritot 21a–21b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf continues excluding categories from the Torah's blood prohibition — creeping animals, eggs, fish, grasshoppers — before turning to include one unusual case: the koy, an animal of uncertain domesticated/undomesticated status, whose blood, fat, carcass, and sciatic nerve are all shown to be forbidden through a chain of derivations. The Gemara then works through the generalization-detail-generalization exegesis that defines exactly which creatures' blood the Torah forbids, and confronts an apparent contradiction about whether human flesh, while a person is alive, can become susceptible to the 'light' impurity that applies to ordinary food. The daf closes with several marginal rulings — when collected fish blood becomes suspect, when creeping-animal blood earns lashes, and whether human blood carries even a preference to abstain — plus the technical rules for combining a sliver of animal carcass with ordinary food to reach the minimum measure for impurity.

slides.title: 🦌 The Koy's Extended Prohibitions
slides.subtitle: A creature of uncertain category (domesticated? undomesticated?) still ends up fully regulated

steps.content: 1️⃣ Blood: included via 'so too every item' in the generalization-detail-generalization reading — Rav Adda bar Avin identifies this as covering the koy specifically, since it's a genuinely distinct category, not mere uncertainty
2️⃣ Fat: derived from the extra word 'kol' ('all fat') in Leviticus 7:23
3️⃣ Carcass: derived from the extra word 'kol' ('all carcasses') in Deuteronomy 14:21
4️⃣ Sciatic nerve: since the Torah ties this prohibition to having a 'spoon of the thigh' (Gen. 32:33), and the koy has one, the prohibition applies automatically
5️⃣ Impurity and the need for ritual slaughter: no specific verse — derived by sheer logic, since the Torah treats the koy like a domesticated animal in every other regard

callout.label: Method shift:
callout.text: Four of these five prohibitions rest on close textual readings; the last relies purely on consistency — once treated like a domesticated animal everywhere else, it must be one here too.

slides.title: 🐓 Why 'Bird AND Animal'? The Generalization-Detail Exegesis
slides.subtitle: Testing why the verse needs both terms, not just one

nodes.content: ❓ Why does the verse specify BOTH 'bird' and 'animal' rather than just one?

🐄 If only 'animal' were written: one might think the prohibition applies only to creatures like an animal — NOT subject to diverse-kinds crossbreeding (kilayim) restrictions on WOOL specifically — excluding birds' feathers from that comparison
🐦 If only 'bird' were written: one might exclude non-kosher birds' blood (since the 'mother bird' mitzva doesn't apply to them) — so 'animal' is added to correct this too

📖 Overall structure: 'no manner of blood' (generalization) → 'bird or animal' (detail) → 'that soul shall be cut off' (generalization again) — a classic generalization-detail-generalization reading, limiting the prohibition to creatures sharing the detail's defining traits

✅ Objection resolved: though the two generalizations carry different penalties (lashes vs. karet), the school of Rabbi Yishmael still applies this exegetical method even across mismatched severity levels

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: Only creatures combining light+severe impurity, forbidden/permitted status, and 'meat' classification fall under the blood prohibition — precisely birds and animals (and, per the extension, the koy).

slides.title: 🧑 Does Human Flesh Ever Carry 'Light' Impurity?
slides.subtitle: A mishna about cutting flesh from a living person seems to contradict the baraita's claim

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: Human blood is excluded from the Torah's prohibition because people lack 'light' (food) impurity — only the severe impurity of a corpse applies to them.

lines.speaker: Challenge
lines.text: But a mishna (Oktzin) says flesh cut from a LIVING person becomes impure as food, given intent to eat it plus contact with liquid — that's exactly 'light' impurity!

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: The baraita's claim applies only after death — a corpse carries only severe impurity, no longer susceptible to food-impurity at all. While alive, flesh CAN become impure as food.

lines.speaker: Further challenge
lines.text: But animal carcasses carry severe impurity too (both flesh and blood, per Beit Hillel) — so why does the baraita treat animals as having 'light' impurity but not humans?

lines.speaker: Final resolution
lines.text: The distinction matters for a specific mishna: non-kosher carcasses (or kosher birds in villages) require explicit INTENT to be eaten before becoming impure as food — but a human corpse, even wrapped to preserve it, NEVER counts as food, since 'his intention is overridden by everyone else's,' as people simply don't eat corpses.

callout.label: Underlying idea:
callout.text: 'Light' impurity for food always requires the item to be a realistic candidate for eating — something categorically true of animal meat but never true of a human body.

slides.title: 🩸 Marginal Cases: Fish Blood, Human Blood, Creeping Things
slides.subtitle: Precise rulings that hinge on collection, warning, and identifying marks

boxes.title: Rav: collected fish blood
items: Fish/grasshopper blood is normally permitted outright
But once COLLECTED in a container without visible scales, it's prohibited — it now LOOKS like forbidden animal/bird blood
If scales are visibly present, it remains permitted even collected

boxes.title: Rabbi Zeira: creeping-animal blood
items: If warned specifically about the 'creeping animal' prohibition (which includes its blood), lashes apply
If warned specifically about the separate 'blood' prohibition, NO lashes — that prohibition doesn't cover this blood at all

boxes.title: Rav Sheshet: human blood
items: Human blood carries not even a preference to abstain from it ab initio
Contrasted with blood of the spleen/heart/kidneys, which — though not punished by karet — still carry a real prohibition

callout.label: Common thread:
callout.text: Each ruling depends on a precise legal technicality — what the item looks like, what prohibition was specified in the warning, or whether any prohibition applies at all.

slides.title: 🍞 Combining Less Than an Olive-Bulk
slides.subtitle: A sliver of animal carcass, too small alone to transmit impurity, still counts when combined with food
rows: Less than an olive-bulk of carcass, combined with less than an egg-bulk of food, together reaching a full egg-bulk — becomes susceptible to food impurity, requiring the added intent (machshava)
Shouldn't this combination also require contact with LIQUID (hekhsher) to become susceptible, per the general rule for items lacking severe impurity?
No — since this carcass sliver COULD eventually combine to a full olive-bulk (triggering severe impurity), it's treated differently from ordinary food and needs no liquid contact

Even a full olive-bulk carcass, if wrapped in less-than-egg-bulk dough, still needs the combination logic — since wrapping blocks contact-impurity but not carrying-impurity, distinguishing it from a wrapped human corpse (whose severe impurity 'breaks through' any wrapping)

callout.label: The corpse contrast:
callout.text: A human corpse's severe impurity 'breaks through and ascends, breaks through and descends' even when wrapped — a stringency with no parallel in animal carcass law, reinforcing why humans and animals are treated so differently throughout this sugya.

summary.principle: The Torah's blood prohibition is drawn with exacting precision — extending by careful derivation to unusual cases like the koy, excluded by defining traits from humans, fish, and creeping things, and hedged by technical rules about collection, intent, and combination that determine exactly when a marginal case crosses into liability.

flowSteps.content: 🦌 The koy's blood, fat, carcass, and sciatic nerve are each derived as forbidden through a distinct textual or logical chain
🐓 A generalization-detail-generalization reading of the blood verses defines exactly which creatures are covered
🧑 Human flesh can carry 'light' food-impurity while alive, but never after death — resolving an apparent contradiction

columns.content: 🩸 Fish, human, and creeping-animal blood each carry their own precise, narrow rulings
🍞 Sub-measure carcass pieces combine with food under carefully defined conditions

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: even a prohibition's outer boundaries are drawn with the same textual precision as its core — nothing is included or excluded without a specific derivation

quiz.q: According to Rav Adda bar Avin, what does the phrase 'so too every item' in the generalization-detail-generalization reading come to include, beyond birds and animals?
o: Fish blood
The blood of a koy, since it is a genuinely distinct category of creature, not merely an uncertain case
Human blood
The blood of creeping animals
quiz.e: Rav Adda bar Avin explains that this phrase includes the koy's blood, understanding the koy as a distinct entity in its own right (not merely an animal of uncertain status), which is why a special verse was needed to include it.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara resolve the apparent contradiction between the baraita (claiming human flesh has no 'light' impurity) and the mishna in Oktzin (which describes flesh cut from a living person becoming impure as food)?
o: The mishna is rejected as unreliable
The baraita's claim applies only after death — a living person's flesh can become impure as food, but a corpse carries only severe impurity
Human flesh never becomes impure under any circumstances
The mishna is discussing animal flesh, not human flesh
quiz.e: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by limiting the baraita's claim to a person's status after death; while alive, flesh cut from a person can indeed become susceptible to the 'light' impurity of food, given proper intent and contact with liquid.

quiz.q: According to Rav, when does fish blood become prohibited for consumption despite normally being entirely permitted?
o: Whenever a person touches it
When it is collected in a receptacle without any visible identifying marks like scales, since it then resembles forbidden animal or bird blood
Fish blood is never prohibited under any circumstances
Only on Yom Kippur
quiz.e: Rav rules that fish blood collected in a container becomes suspect and prohibited unless it contains visible scales confirming its fish origin, since otherwise it could be mistaken for forbidden blood.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Zeira, under what condition is one flogged for consuming the blood of a creeping animal?
o: Never, under any circumstances
Only if warned specifically about the prohibition against eating a creeping animal (which encompasses its blood), not if warned about the general blood prohibition
Only if warned about the general blood prohibition
Always, regardless of the warning given
quiz.e: Rabbi Zeira explains that lashes apply only when the forewarning specifies the creeping-animal prohibition, which includes its blood; the general blood prohibition does not actually cover creeping animals' blood at all.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Ḥiyya's explanation, why doesn't a sliver of animal carcass (less than an olive-bulk) combined with less than an egg-bulk of food require contact with liquid to become susceptible to impurity, unlike ordinary food items?
o: Because carcasses are never susceptible to any impurity
Because since this sliver could eventually combine to reach a full olive-bulk (triggering severe impurity on its own), it is treated differently from ordinary food that never carries severe impurity
Because liquid never affects susceptibility to impurity
Because dough always eliminates the need for liquid contact
quiz.e: Rabbi Ḥiyya explains that because this carcass sliver has the potential to eventually reach the threshold for severe impurity on its own, it is exempted from the general rule requiring liquid contact for susceptibility, unlike ordinary food that could never carry severe impurity.
